questions.questionText: You receive a text message from an unknown number containing a suspicious link and urging you to act immediately. What is the safest action to take?

options.text: Tap the link to see where it leads.
Delete the message, report it, and do not click any links.
Forward the message to 10 friends.
Call the unknown number and insult the caller.

questions.explanation: Refraining from interaction and deleting/reporting the message mitigates risk.

questions.questionText: You receive an unexpected text in a familiar bank-message thread. Does the existing thread or familiar sender ID prove that the new text is genuine?

options.text: True
False

questions.explanation: Sender IDs can be spoofed, including in an existing message thread. Verify an unexpected request using the bank's official app, website, or published phone number.

questions.questionText: What does the term "Smishing" stand for?

options.text: Secure Mail Phishing
SMS Phishing (Short Message Service Phishing)
Software Management Phishing
System Media Injection

questions.explanation: Smishing combines "SMS" (text messaging) and "phishing".

questions.questionText: You receive a text message: "USPS Alert: Your package cannot be delivered due to an incorrect house number. Update info here: bit.ly/3xY9zQ". You are expecting a package. What is the correct action?

options.text: Tap the link immediately and enter your home address.
Do not tap the link; open your official USPS app or browser bookmark independently to track the package.
Reply "STOP" to check if the sender is real.
Text back your credit card details.

questions.explanation: Always verify parcel delivery alerts by accessing the official website or app independently, never through unsolicited SMS links.

questions.questionText: You should never send a one-time verification code to someone who asks for it in a text message.

options.text: True
False

questions.explanation: The lesson says verification codes protect accounts and should not be shared with someone who asks for them.

questions.questionText: What shortcode number can users in many regions forward spam or smishing texts to for reporting?

options.text: 7726 (SPAM)

questions.explanation: Forwarding spam texts to 7726 (SPAM) alerts carriers to investigate and block malicious sender numbers.

questions.questionText: An unknown WhatsApp contact claims to be from your company's IT team and sends an unexpected work-access link. How should you respond?

options.text: Install it immediately because the message displays the company logo
Do not follow the link; verify the request through a known work contact and report the message
Reply and ask the sender to send a second link that looks more familiar
Call a number supplied in the unexpected message to confirm the request

questions.explanation: The lesson advises verifying unexpected work-access messages through known work channels instead of following unsolicited links.

questions.questionText: An attacker may trigger a real one-time code and then send a text asking you to share that code.

options.text: True
False

questions.explanation: The lesson's OTP-grab example explains that an attacker can trigger a real code and then ask the recipient to send it.

questions.questionText: You attempt to log into your work portal. A minute later, you receive a text: "IT Helpdesk: We detected an abnormal login. Reply YES with the code you just received to block the login." What is happening?

options.text: IT is securely helping you protect your account.
An attacker triggered your real login prompt and is trying to trick you into texting them your OTP.
Your phone has a hardware virus that generates text messages.
Your mobile service provider is upgrading its network towers.

questions.explanation: Attackers trigger a real login prompt to generate a genuine OTP, then smish the victim to forward that OTP to complete the breach.

questions.questionText: What technology allows scammers to change the phone number or name displayed on your mobile incoming text screen?

options.text: OAuth 2.0
Caller ID / Alpha-Numeric Sender ID Spoofing
Transport Layer Security
Fiber Optic Splicing

questions.explanation: Sender ID spoofing allows SMS gateways to modify the header sender text displayed on receiver phones.

questions.questionText: If a text message appears in the same chat thread as previous legitimate bank messages, it is 100% guaranteed to be safe.

options.text: True
False

questions.explanation: Attackers can use Sender ID spoofing to inject fake text messages into existing SMS conversation threads on mobile devices.

questions.questionText: Why are mobile browsers particularly vulnerable to web link deceptive techniques?

options.text: Mobile screens automatically block HTTPS connections.
Mobile screens have limited space, often truncating or hiding the full URL bar and security indicators.
Smartphones cannot run web browsers.
Mobile networks disable domain name resolution.

questions.explanation: Reduced screen size makes it difficult for users to inspect the full domain path of a link before interacting.

questions.questionText: Which of the following are primary indicators of a smishing attempt? *(Select TWO)*

options.text: A text says a package cannot be delivered and asks you to follow a shortened link to update your address.
A text claiming to be from the IT desk asks you to reply with a 6-digit MFA code.
A calendar reminder created locally on your phone.
An internal Slack message from a verified colleague.

questions.explanation: The lesson shows a fake parcel-delivery text with a shortened link and warns never to share an MFA code requested by text.

questions.questionText: What is the risk of using shortened URLs (bit.ly, tinyurl) in SMS messages?

options.text: They consume extra mobile data.
They obscure the actual destination domain, making it impossible to evaluate safety at a glance.
They automatically install viruses without user interaction.
They disable mobile touchscreen responsiveness.

questions.explanation: URL shorteners hide the real destination address, concealing malicious domains.

questions.questionText: Personal smartphones used under BYOD (Bring Your Own Device) policies are always protected by corporate firewalls.

options.text: True
False

questions.explanation: Personal BYOD devices operate on commercial cellular networks or home Wi-Fi, bypassing corporate perimeter firewalls.

questions.questionText: A remote worker receives a text message: *"HR ALERT: Update your direct deposit bank details at* *https://payroll-portal-update.com* *before 5 PM to receive this week's paycheck."* What should the worker check first?

options.text: Tap the link and enter the old bank account number.
Verify the URL against official company payroll bookmarks and contact HR via official email/call.
Post a screenshot of the link on personal social media.
Reply with credit card credentials.

questions.explanation: Urgent threats regarding payroll/direct deposit sent via text require out-of-band verification.

questions.questionText: What should you do if a text asks you to provide a one-time code for a work account?

options.text: Reply only if the text displays your company's logo
Open the link in the message to check whether the request is real
Do not share the code; verify the request through an official app or known work channel
Forward the code to a coworker to check whether it is valid

questions.explanation: The lesson warns not to share one-time codes and recommends checking unexpected work-account requests through trusted channels.

questions.questionText: A text message reads: *"Bank Alert: Fraud detected. Call 1-800-555-0199 immediately to cancel the transaction."* What is the safest way to call your bank?

options.text: Call the 1-800 number provided in the text message.
Call the customer service number printed on the back of your official payment card or official site.
Wait 3 weeks and check your mailbox.
Text the number back asking for the caller's name.

questions.explanation: The lesson recommends verifying a bank alert through a published number or the bank's official site rather than relying on contact details in an unexpected text.

questions.questionText: Which TWO risks can make a smishing link harder to assess on a personal phone than on a company-managed laptop?

options.text: Personal phones may not have the same web filtering or endpoint protection as company-managed laptops.
Smartphones cannot connect to the internet.
Small screens or in-app browsers can make the actual link destination harder to inspect.
SMS messages are encrypted with zero-trust protocols by default.

questions.explanation: The lesson notes that personal phones may have less web filtering or endpoint protection, and that small screens or in-app browsers can make destinations harder to inspect.

questions.questionText: Legitimate logistics companies will always require you to pay a re-delivery fee via a third-party link sent by SMS.

options.text: True
False

questions.explanation: Demanding credit card details via SMS links for "unclaimed parcels" is a standard smishing lure.
